## The idea

By the end of a capstone, several pieces of code have begun to recur: event
playback, bar validation, transposition, chord voicing, articulation, and source
reporting. Repetition is evidence for a library only after the helper's inputs
and behaviour have become stable. Extracting it earlier can turn a provisional
decision into an API that every later piece must work around.

Complete at least one of Lessons 55–57 before this refactor. A finished project
provides actual call sites, awkward events, and provenance fields against which
an abstraction can be judged. Without those examples, a library design mostly
records expectations about music you have not yet represented.

Choose one event schema. Throughout the later lessons, `:note`, `:start`, and
`:duration` form its centre, with `:amp` present when dynamics belong to score
data. Migrate older pieces to that schema instead of asking every helper to
accept `:duration`, `:dur`, and `:length`. Compatibility branches preserve
short-term convenience by placing permanent ambiguity in future code.

Keep the framework small enough that a score remains readable. A helper should
remove repeated machinery while leaving musical decisions visible at the call
site. Write the README for a future reader who remembers Ruby but no longer
remembers why starts are absolute, how rests are represented, or which layer
controls articulation.

## Run this

This fresh buffer presents a small candidate library beside one theme that uses
it. Validation, transposition, and rendering all accept the same event shape,
so their contracts can be compared without adapters or duplicated score data.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 78

define :validate_events do |events, expected_end|
  raise "empty score" if events.empty?

  events.each do |event|
    required = [:note, :start, :duration]
    missing = required.reject { |key| event.key?(key) }
    raise "missing keys: #{missing}" unless missing.empty?
    raise "duration must be positive" unless event[:duration] > 0
  end

  actual_end = events.map { |event| event[:start] + event[:duration] }.max
  raise "expected end #{expected_end}, got #{actual_end}" unless actual_end == expected_end
end

define :transpose_events do |events, semitones|
  events.map do |event|
    event.merge(note: note(event[:note]) + semitones)
  end
end

define :play_events do |events, synth_name|
  use_synth synth_name
  cursor = 0.0
  events.each do |event|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    play event[:note],
      release: event[:duration] * 0.82,
      amp: event.fetch(:amp, 0.8)
    cursor = event[:start]
  end
  sleep events.last[:duration]
end

theme = [
  {note: :c4, start: 0.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.65},
  {note: :e4, start: 1.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.72},
  {note: :g4, start: 2.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.8},
  {note: :c5, start: 3.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.9}
]

validate_events theme, 4.0
play_events theme, :piano
sleep 1
play_events transpose_events(theme, 7), :pluck
```

The piano states C, E, G, C in a rising arpeggio. The pluck repeats the same
shape seven semitones higher. `transpose_events` returns new hashes through
`merge`, so the original theme remains available for playback and comparison
after the transformed version has been created.

## Change one thing

1. Remove `:duration` from one event. Validation reports the missing contract
   field before playback begins. Restore it, then add an unrelated key such as
   `:phrase`. A helper should ignore extension data it does not need while still
   enforcing the fields on which its own result depends.
2. Make `transpose_events` assign directly to `event[:note]`, then return
   `event` explicitly from the `map` block. The transposed phrase may sound
   correct, but the original array has also moved, so later playback no longer
   offers a baseline. If you omit the explicit `event`, Ruby returns the assigned
   number and the renderer receives integers instead of hashes. Restore `merge`
   and confirm that transformation leaves source data intact.
3. Add an `:articulation` key and a narrow helper mapping `:legato`, `:detached`,
   and `:accent` to release or amplitude options. Keep note conversion, start
   handling, and duration validation outside it. The helper's name and inputs
   should describe one responsibility.

## Why it works

A small library gives repeated representations one authority. If every score
uses `:duration`, a correction to duration validation can serve them all. If
transposition always returns new events, callers know that their source array
remains suitable for comparison. A few predictable contracts offer more value
than a large collection of wrappers whose effects must be rediscovered at each
call site.

Names should reveal the abstraction level. `play_events` renders a general
absolute timeline. `play_phrase` suits a sequential array in which every event
follows the previous duration. A voicing helper embodies a harmonic policy and
should remain local until several pieces genuinely need that same policy. Code
used once may be clear where it stands.

README prose should explain decisions rather than translate function names into
sentences. Record why starts are absolute, whether amplitude belongs to score or
performance data, how rests occupy time, how ties become sounding events, and
which Sonic Pi version the examples target. Include one fresh-buffer program
small enough to expose the complete workflow, followed by the manual listening
checks that automated tests cannot perform.

Version the library beside the pieces that depend on it. A schema migration
should be visible both in helper code and in the score data moved to the new
shape. Supporting several aliases indefinitely avoids one explicit migration
at the cost of branching in every validator, renderer, and transformation that
follows.

The capability at the end of the book remains musical and practical: take a
printed score or short recording, represent it as editable code, render it, and
explain the theory visible in the data. The library reduces the repeated work
around that process. It should never obscure the pitches, timings, sources, and
interpretive choices that constitute the process itself.

## Take it further

Collect helpers that already appear in at least three finished pieces. Produce
one small library file and one README, then migrate two older scores to the
settled schema. Include event validation, `play_events`, transposition, and one
articulation or voicing function. Read each migrated score without opening the
helpers: its musical structure and important decisions should still be visible.
Run and record Ruby syntax and automated validation results, and list the Sonic
Pi comparisons that remain manual QA rather than describing them as already
heard.
